senses.gloss:
ajina
------------------------------------------
Ajina is skin in general and the skin of a black antelope in particular. Hence the name कृष्णाजिन. Throughout the ages it has been a symbol of holiness and Vedic culture. Even the country आर्यावर्त, has been defined as the territory where kṛṣṇamṛga or the black antelope wanders freely. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.1.4. 1-2) compares यज्ञ (sacrifice) to a black antelope with white, black and yellow hair representing respectively the Ṛk, सामन् and Yajus.
Being considered holy, it is often used in sacrificial rites for various purposes as in husking grains from which cakes are made.
It is used by the ब्रह्मचारिन् (celibate novice pursuing the Vedic studies) and the यति or मुनि (ascetic) as a seat or spread or a couch.
A strip of कृष्णाजिन used to be worn by the dvijas in the earlier days as यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread) which was later replaced by the thread.

Ājīvakas
(‘life-longers,’ ‘mendicants’)
------------------------------------------
India has been a land of अस्चेतिच्स् and asceticism since millennia. The आजीवकस् (sometimes misspelt as ājīvikas also) a group of such अस्चेतिच्स् mentioned in the edicts of अशोक pillars seem to be an ancient order of some standing.
According to their tradition नन्द-vatsa, Kṛśa-Sāṅkṛtyāyana and Maṅkhalī-putta or मस्करिन् Gośāla are the three great teachers from whom the sect originated and got stabilised. Historians believe that Gośāla was a younger contemporary of महावीर, the last of Jaina Tīrthaṅkaras. Jaina texts like the Uvāsagadasāo graphically describe the conflict between them triggered off by the desertion of Saddāla-putta of the Ājīvaka sect who went over to the Nirgrantha sect of Māhāvīra.
Not much is known of the doctrines of this sect. They practised severe auste-rities and were probably followers of हठयोग and occultism. That they might have lived in caves is suggested by the inscriptions of अशोक mentioning the dedications of cave-dwellings for their use in the Barabar hills of Bihar. They might have practised nudity.
Ghurye feels that the sect had a होउसे-holder section also (G. S. Ghurye, Indian Sādhus, Bombay, Popular Prakashan, 1953, p. 36).
Except for some references in Buddhist works like the Dīgha Nikāya, there is practically no literature left about their philosophy. They were probably fatalists, agnostics or even atheists.
Whatever might have been their philosophy, they once commanded respect and influence in the society and were rivals of the Jaina अस्चेतिच्स्.
Practice of unsocial customs, perhaps cost them their popularity.

ajīva
(‘the non-living or inanimate’)
------------------------------------------
Jaina metaphysics divides द्रव्य or substance into two broad groups: astikāya (that which has a body and hence extended in space) and anastikāya (that which has no body). The astikāyas are again sub-divided into जीव (animate) and अजीव (inanimate). अजीव is further subdivided into धर्म (the medium necessary for motion), अधर्म (medium necessary for rest or immobility), आकाश (space) and pudgala (matter).
